source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: Pavlovian pruning of decision trees
finding: People stop mentally evaluating a sequence once it hits a large loss. The pruning does not shrink when it becomes costly.
numbers: N=46 in three groups (15, 16, 15) by size of large loss (-70, -100, -140). Sequences of 2-8 moves. Pruning was costly in the -70 and -100 groups, free in -140. Specific pruning did not differ by group.
quote: curtailed any further evaluation of a sequence as soon as they encountered a large loss
limits: One lab, healthy volunteers, deterministic 6-state task with symbolic payoffs. Model-based inference, not direct observation of thought.
agent_relevance: Rule for the agent: after a bad first step, do not drop the branch automatically. Require a check that looks past the loss before cutting.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: Pavlovian pruning of decision trees
finding: The full look-ahead model alone predicted 77% of choices. The best model (pruning plus learned Pavlovian values) predicted about 91%.
numbers: Look-ahead predictive probability 0.71. Habitual SARSA model was far worse than the goal-directed discount model (BIC gain 314). Specific pruning exceeded general pruning in 14/15, 12/16 and 14/15 subjects.
limits: Model comparison depends on the model set the authors built. No pre-registration.
agent_relevance: Humans are mostly goal-directed planners with a loss-triggered stopping rule on top. A scaffold can model this as a stop chance after a loss.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: Pavlovian pruning of decision trees
finding: Pruning is not just loss aversion. Models with separate reward and loss weights still needed the pruning term.
numbers: Punishments weighted about 1.4 times rewards. Adding loss aversion to the best pruning model did not improve parsimony. Pruning plus Loss beat Discount plus Loss.
limits: Loss weights inferred jointly with pruning, so some trade-off is possible.
agent_relevance: Two separate faults in an agent: overweighting a bad step, and not looking past it. Fix them separately.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: Pavlovian pruning of decision trees
finding: Pruning grows with depth. Early large losses were passed through, deeper ones were avoided.
numbers: Depth 4-5: the optimal sequence was chosen more often if the loss came in the first half than in the second half. At depth 6 or more no difference (few events). With one move left, about 40% of choices in state 6 still went to the formerly rewarded state 1, which was wrong.
limits: Few deep events. The depth effect comes partly from how the two pruning parameters interact, not from a built-in rule.
agent_relevance: Pruning risk is highest in big trees. Apply the check-before-cut rule hardest at depth.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: Pavlovian pruning of decision trees
finding: Mood link: specific pruning correlated with subclinical depression score (BDI) but general pruning did not.
numbers: Weighted regression controlling age, sex, verbal IQ, working memory and NEO traits. Reward sensitivity correlated negatively with BDI but did not survive correction. No link with neuroticism. 94% of subjects had low BDI.
limits: Healthy, low-BDI sample. Later studies did not reproduce this correlation (see b11, b12, b15).
agent_relevance: Do not build the agent around the mood correlation. It is not reliable.

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies
finding: Replication in a new sample (N=37) with a harder, time-pressured version. Pruning stayed after controlling for chunking of sequences and reuse of earlier sequences.
numbers: 1 - gammaS < 1 - gammaG for 37/37 subjects. General discounting (gammaG) was indistinguishable from zero once fragmentation was modelled, so generic early stopping was mostly a side effect of chunking.
quote: every subject discounted outcomes distant to large losses more steeply
limits: Same lab and task family. Fragment analysis uses a 24-25 parameter model.
agent_relevance: Loss-specific pruning is real. Generic early stopping may be explained by subgoals. Tell the agent to chunk into subgoals, not to stop at random.

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies
finding: People break problems into subgoal fragments and reuse them. This cut the cost by more than half in the worked example.
numbers: Fragments ended in the salient state 2 for 90% of target end states (range 0.83-0.99), above chance in every subject. A depth-3 tree costs 24 additions; fragmenting into depth 2 plus depth 1 costs 10. Fragment length did not correlate with verbal IQ (rho=0.08, P=0.64).
limits: The task has no true bottleneck state, so subgoals were driven by salient reward.
agent_relevance: Subgoal decomposition is a rival way to cut trees that needs no loss trigger. Prefer it to loss-triggered pruning.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Independent fMRI sample reproduces behavioural pruning with large effect sizes.
numbers: N=37 analysed (41 recruited, 1 excluded for substance history). Optimal sequence without a large loss was chosen 78% (SD 18); with a large loss in it 37% (SD 18). Difference 41%, t(36)=12.51, d=2.06. The gap grew with depth: 34% at depth 3 (d=1.36), 40% at depth 4 (d=1.86), 49% at depth 5 (d=1.70).
limits: Same lab. Participants were students.
agent_relevance: Size to expect: an agent that prunes will lose about half of its correct paths through a loss when the tree is deep.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: The pruning model beat the discount model decisively. Loss-aversion extension added little.
numbers: Delta iBIC pruning vs discount = 77.5. Pruning+loss vs pruning = 5.8. Variance explained 41.7% (lookahead), 52.5% (discount), 54.4% (pruning), 55.3% (pruning+loss). gammaG > gammaS: t(36)=5.12, d=0.84.
limits: Loss terms gave a smaller gain than in the 2012 sample.
agent_relevance: Confirms the loss-specific stop is the main added piece over generic depth limits.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Brain basis: subgenual cingulate (SGC) activity rose with model-derived inclination to prune, more so on harder trials.
numbers: SGC peak MNI -6,29,-2, t(36)=3.87, pSVC=0.004. Interaction with difficulty at -6,35,-5, t(36)=3.47, pSVC=0.009. Planning and valuation used separate networks. Insula and DLPFC responses to receiving large losses correlated with overall pruning.
limits: Small-volume corrected within a region; display threshold p<0.005 uncorrected. Reverse inference risk.
agent_relevance: Suggests pruning is a separate affective gate, not part of planning itself. Keep the gate as a separate code step.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Pruning was faster than other errors and more common on harder problems, so it saves effort. The depression link did not replicate.
numbers: State anxiety (not depression or trait anxiety) predicted the gap between no-large-loss and large-loss accuracy, t(37)=2.12, p=0.042. The model pruning estimate (gammaG - gammaS) correlated with no questionnaire. Authors: not replicated the correlation with subclinical depression.
quote: we did not replicate our previous finding
limits: State anxiety link is p=0.042 in a regression with several predictors, uncorrected.
agent_relevance: Pruning is a cost-saving shortcut. The agent should pay the saved effort back with a check when stakes are high.

source: A comparison of 'pruning' during multi-step planning in depressed and healthy individuals (2022, Psychological Medicine)
finding: Failed test of the depression theory: unmedicated depressed adults pruned as much as healthy adults.
numbers: N=30 depressed vs 31 healthy. gammaS: t(59)=0.320, p=0.750, BF10=0.272. Total money won: t(59)=0.345, p=0.731. BDI vs gammaS in depressed: r=0.068, p=0.748, BF10=0.261. Mean BDI 25.44 vs 3.00.
quote: We found no evidence that sub-optimal pruning is evident in depression
limits: Patients had mild to moderate depression and were in low-intensity care. Bayes factors for some contrasts were inconclusive (BF10 0.4-0.5).
agent_relevance: Mood-based pruning claims are weak. Do not tune the agent by mood analogies.

source: A comparison of 'pruning' during multi-step planning in depressed and healthy individuals (2022, Psychological Medicine)
finding: Healthy controls again pruned strongly. Large-gain weight was about three times the large-loss weight, so no classic loss aversion.
numbers: Specific pruning parameter about 0.6 in both groups, as in Lally 2017 and slightly above Huys 2012. Reward weight +140 = 7.25 vs -140 = -2.60 (healthy). The learned Pavlovian state term did not help here, unlike in 2012.
limits: The extra Pavlovian state-attraction parameter lost parsimony here, so that part of the 2012 result did not replicate.
agent_relevance: The core pruning effect is robust across at least three samples. The learned-state attraction is not.

source: A comparison of 'pruning' during multi-step planning in depressed and healthy individuals (2022, Psychological Medicine)
finding: Task details reproduced across labs.
numbers: 48 trials of 2-8 moves, half with plan-ahead entry. Payoffs: ++ 1.40 pounds, + 20p, - 20p, -- 1.40 pounds. Training had to pass a transition test before the task.
limits: Small stakes. Large-stake behaviour not tested.
agent_relevance: The task can be turned into an LLM benchmark of loss-triggered cutting.

source: A comparison of 'pruning' during multi-step planning in depressed and healthy individuals (2022, Psychological Medicine)
finding: The authors list reasons for the failed depression result and note the earlier correlation was never reproduced.
numbers: The earlier BDI link was in healthy people, not patients, and did not appear in Huys 2015 or Lally 2017 either. They suggest milder severity and low-intensity treatment as causes.
limits: Authors speculate; no test of these reasons.
agent_relevance: The mood-link claim failed in 2015, 2017 and 2022. Count it as unsupported.

source: Computational mechanisms underlying multi-step planning deficits in methamphetamine use disorder (2025, Transl Psychiatry)
finding: Pruning is stronger in methamphetamine use disorder: more pruning and fewer points.
numbers: N=40 users vs 49 controls. Aversive pruning 0.33 vs 0.15, F(1,100)=16.46, d=0.81. Large-loss discounting 0.49 vs 0.33, d=0.74. Points won 2034 vs 3145, d=0.77. Accuracy on no-large-loss trials equal (F=0.33, p=0.568). Correct on optimal-large-loss trials 19% vs 35%.
limits: Cross-sectional. Users were in treatment. Female participants pruned more (F(1,84)=5.98, p=0.017).
agent_relevance: Pruning differences are specific to paths through losses and do not harm general planning. Test an agent on both trial types.

source: Computational mechanisms underlying multi-step planning deficits in methamphetamine use disorder (2025, Transl Psychiatry)
finding: An anxiety induction did not raise pruning. Users pruned slightly less under breathing resistance.
numbers: Resistance effect not significant on any parameter (Fs <= 3.68, ps >= 0.058). Group x Resistance on pruning F(1,90)=5.17, p=0.025. Craving change predicted pruning in users.
limits: Interaction p=0.025 uncorrected. The induction worked on self-report but not on pruning.
agent_relevance: Acute stress is not a reliable booster of pruning, so do not assume pressure triggers it in the agent.

source: Computational mechanisms underlying multi-step planning deficits in methamphetamine use disorder (2025, Transl Psychiatry)
finding: Pruning can be measured cleanly and higher pruning means worse payoff.
numbers: Parameter recovery r >= 0.91 for each parameter. Difference score pi = gammaG - gammaS. Simulations: higher pruning gave fewer points at fixed reward sensitivity and general discounting. Controls for working memory and memory of path values were run.
limits: Supplement details not read.
agent_relevance: An LLM version can be scored with the same parameter.

source: Mahajan et al. (2025) Balancing safety and efficiency in human decision making (eLife)
finding: Model: a fixed Pavlovian avoidance bias blocks value discovery behind pain. A bias gated by outcome uncertainty keeps safety and loses little efficiency.
numbers: Grid-world simulations. T-maze: reward +0.1 left vs +1 right, at least -0.5 damage on the way right. As fixed bias grew, value propagation toward the +1 goal fell. Human VR test N=28 (14 female, mean age 27.96) approach-withdraw task with shocks. The flexible model fit choices and reaction times best.
limits: The human test is a simple approach-withdraw task, not planning, with small N. The authors call it a basic test.
agent_relevance: Supports a gate whose strength shrinks as the world becomes predictable. Be cautious early, looser later.

source: Sezener, Dezfouli, Keramati (2019) Optimizing the depth and the direction of prospective planning using information values
finding: Rational rival: stop expanding a branch when the expected gain from deeper search is smaller than the time cost. Time pressure reduces depth.
numbers: Simulations in a grid world. Cited human data: decision limits of 2000 ms vs 700 ms. The 700 ms group planned to a shallower depth and switched to habit values sooner. Mean-based and variance-based pruning compared with the information-value rule.
limits: Simulation plus cited data, no new human experiment. The model has no loss-specific pruning.
agent_relevance: Rival to Pavlovian pruning: cut by value of information, not by valence. Our code can use this as the stopping rule.

source: Disentangling the component processes in complex planning impairments following vmPFC lesion (2025, J Neurosci)
finding: Value-threshold pruning is a standard part of planning models. In a game task, vmPFC lesions reduced search depth.
numbers: Four-in-a-Row: 18 lesion patients vs 30 healthy controls. Two-Step: 49 patients vs 20 controls, no group difference. The model prunes moves below best-minus-threshold, citing Huys 2012. Groups were summarised by depth, heuristic quality and feature drop, not by pruning threshold.
limits: Value-gap pruning differs from loss-triggered pruning. The paper does not test loss triggers.
agent_relevance: Value-gap pruning is the normal tree-search rule and is a different thing from pruning after one bad step.

source: Qian et al. (2026) PAC-CF: Calibrating irreversible frontier pruning in LLM-guided search
finding: LLM-guided search: pruning on an evaluator score is irreversible and biased, so a calibrated threshold is needed.
numbers: Three domains (Game24 N=100, Blocksworld N=99, GTA N=99), five controllers, budgets B100-B500. For ToolTree, +4.38 utility points at each budget. Physical requests down 18.94-18.95%, tokens down 23.57-23.76%. Coverage target Q=0.95, evaluator repeats R=4.
limits: Preprint. The abstract gives no false-prune rate. The utility gain is for one controller.
agent_relevance: Direct parallel: a language-model scorer may cut the right branch. Calibrate cuts on held-out tasks.

source: Qian et al. (2026) PAC-CF: Calibrating irreversible frontier pruning in LLM-guided search
finding: Uncalibrated top-K pruning removes the correct path often when the evaluator is noisy.
numbers: TSP50 stress test, 16 evaluator repeats: fixed top-K=4 removed 64.4% of reference actions on conflict frontiers and 52.1% on control frontiers. K=6: 39.1% and 24.0%. Full reference path preserved in 0/24 (K=4) and 1/24 (K=6) conflict instances. With PAC-CF at B100, path survival was 97.46% on Game24 and 99.80% on Blocksworld.
limits: TSP is not one of the three LLM benchmarks. Survival rates are descriptive diagnostics, not guarantees.
agent_relevance: Unverified cuts lose answers. Never prune on a score alone (guardrails G3, G5).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Tree of Thoughts: search with self-evaluation and backtracking raises success on a task where early choices matter.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: chain of thought 4%, Tree of Thoughts 74%.
limits: The page gave only two headline figures. Self-evaluation used the model as judge, which our schema forbids.
agent_relevance: Search over branches beats a single path, but branch cuts should be checked by code.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head: Pavlovian pruning of decision trees
finding: The authors tie the result to a serotonin and behavioural-inhibition account of depression. This was not tested.
numbers: They cite a report that acute tryptophan depletion did not impair the Tower of London task, which has no obvious aversive point for pruning.
quote: We plan to test this directly in future studies
limits: No pharmacological test in this paper.
agent_relevance: Treat the serotonin story as a hypothesis only.

source: Mahajan et al. (2025) Balancing safety and efficiency in human decision making (eLife)
finding: Pavlovian avoidance helps safety early but costs value discovery later: a safety-versus-efficiency trade.
numbers: Experiment 2 used fixed omega values to show sampling asymmetry. Higher fixed bias gave lower reward-value propagation to the right goal and more avoidance of punishment.
limits: Simulation only for this claim.
agent_relevance: Suggests an adjustable cut: tighten early, loosen as evidence accumulates.

source: Lally et al. (2017) The neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Pruning appeared with a single large-loss size in the scanner task, matching the size-insensitivity claim.
numbers: Large loss was -70 pence. Model parameter counts: lookahead 1, discount 2, pruning 3, pruning+loss 6. Choice log likelihood 1151 (pruning+loss) vs 1502 (lookahead).
limits: Size sensitivity not retested.
agent_relevance: A small loss was enough to trigger the cut. Expect an agent to cut even on mild setbacks.
